sources.citation: Reinhart, Markey, Laudenbach, Pantusen, Yurko, Weinberg, Brown. Do LLMs write like humans? Variation in grammatical and rhetorical styles. PNAS 122 (2025), e2422455122.

pinned.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 122 (2025), e2422455122, as stated in the arXiv journal reference
pinned.status: peer-reviewed journal article; PNAS page not fetched

sources.target: Whether LLM-generated English differs from human English in grammatical, lexical, and rhetorical style, and whether LLMs differ from each other, using Biber's 66 linguistic categories and author classifiers.
sources.unit_of_analysis: Text chunks in parallel human and LLM corpora; per-text rates of 66 Biber categories.

data.used: HAP-E (six registers: academic, news, fiction, spoken, blogs, TV and movie scripts; 8,290 texts after filtering; 66,320 chunks; 14,535 test chunks), CAP derived from COCA (76,920 chunks), M4 arXiv preprints for generalization; GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini, Llama 3 8B, 70B, and their Instruct variants.
data.availability: unknown; the arXiv HTML shows no repository, availability statement, or code link, only an SI Appendix reference

sources.method: Parallel corpora, Biber tagging, paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction and Cohen's d, random forest and logistic regression author classifiers, out-of-domain test on M4.
relevant_findings: GPT-4o: present participial clauses about 5.3x the human rate (d=1.38), nominalizations 2.1x (d=1.23), that-clauses as subject 2.6x (d=0.77), phrasal coordination 1.9x (d=0.81), agentless passives about half the human rate.
Instruction-tuned models overuse specific words ('tapestry' in 23% and 'amidst' in 27% of GPT-4o outputs).
Pairwise LLM-versus-human random forests reach 93-98% on the parallel corpora and fall to chance on arXiv preprints for Llama base models.
limitations: General registers only; no code comments or technical documentation.
Out-of-domain transfer collapsed on arXiv preprints, so rates are register-specific.
Numbers were read from the arXiv HTML and not rechecked against the PDF.

decision.scope: The grammatical findings become candidate constructions in E1 and E3 where the shared feature contract can express them; participial and that-clause candidates wait for a real dependency backend. Lexical overuse is a candidate for the frozen phrase baseline. Data and classifiers are not reused.
decision.reason: Closest study to the target task: it measures constructions instead of comparing detectors. Its register-specific rates cannot be transferred to technical prose.

sources.citation: Kobak, González-Márquez, Horvát, Lause. Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary. Science Advances 11(27), 2025.

pinned.version: arXiv v5, submitted 2025-07-03 (comments: reverting to v3)
pinned.venue: Science Advances, Vol. 11, No. 27, first published 2025-07-02 (Europe PMC)
pinned.status: peer-reviewed journal article, open access, CC BY per Europe PMC; science.org page not fetched

sources.target: Excess word usage in 2024 PubMed abstracts relative to a counterfactual extrapolated from 2021-2022, and a lower bound on the share of abstracts processed with LLMs by discipline, country, and journal.
sources.unit_of_analysis: Yearly corpus-level word frequency; share of abstracts containing selected excess style words.

data.availability: PubMed bulk download is public; analysis code and a 362,442 x 15 yearly word-occurrence matrix are stated to be at https://github.com/berenslab/llm-excess-vocab (repository not fetched)
data.terms: repository license unknown; article text CC BY

sources.method: Counterfactual expected frequency q = p(-2) + 2 * max{p(-2) - p(-3), 0}, a one-sided projection from the two preceding baseline years that never falls below the last baseline value (arXiv HTML v5, statistical analysis); frequency gap delta = p - q and frequency ratio r = p / q; excess words satisfy delta > 0.01 or log10 r > (log10 2 / 4) * log10 p (arXiv HTML v5, section 2.1); style versus content annotation; lower-bound share from abstracts containing selected style words.
relevant_findings: 454 excess words in 2024 versus 190 during Covid; the 2024 set is dominated by style words.
Examples with values: delves (r=28.0), underscores (r=13.8), showcasing (r=10.7), potential (delta=0.052), findings (delta=0.041), crucial (delta=0.037).
Lower bound of at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts processed with LLMs, up to about 40% in some subcorpora.
limitations: Lower bound only; abstracts without the selected style words are missed.
The method cannot separate causes of a frequency change or attribute a change to one model.
Biomedical abstracts only; no grammatical or rhetorical measures.
The projection floor max{., 0} makes the excess conservative for words whose frequency was falling; an adaptation in E4 must keep that term.

decision.scope: E4 uses the counterfactual-trend method for word and construction frequencies across historical periods and contemporary snapshots. Population-level shifts are reported as prevalence, never as a document label or a share of AI-authored text. Biomedical data is not reused.
decision.reason: A tested temporal method with an explicit lower-bound reading; its domain and its authorship-share estimate do not transfer.

verified_facts: Formulas quoted from https://arxiv.org/html/2406.07016v5 on 2026-09-10: q = p(-2) + 2 * max{p(-2) - p(-3), 0}; excess when delta > 0.01 or log10 r > (log10 2 / 4) * log10 p.

sources.target: Whether widely used GPT detectors misclassify writing by non-native English writers as AI-generated, and whether simple prompting changes the outcome.
sources.unit_of_analysis: Writing samples from native and non-native English writers; genre and counts not on the abstract page.

data.used: Not named on the abstract page.
data.availability: no data or code link on the arXiv page

sources.method: Empirical evaluation of several detectors on the two groups; prompting experiments that both reduce the bias and bypass detectors.
relevant_findings: Detectors consistently misclassify non-native writing samples as AI-generated while native samples are identified (abstract).
The abstract attributes the effect to constrained linguistic expression; no numbers on the page.
limitations: Detector names, sample sizes, and rates were not read.

decision.scope: A named limitation check: any subgroup analysis by language background requires independently confirmed, permitted metadata; no background is inferred from prose or names, and an absent check is recorded as an open limitation, not as absence of bias.
decision.reason: The risk it documents applies directly to lexical-diversity and simplicity features; the study supplies no method to reuse.

sources.unit_of_analysis: Not stated on the abstract page.

data.used: Human text and outputs of 11 LLMs; genres and human corpora not named on the page.
data.availability: no data or code link on the arXiv page

sources.method: Large-scale feature analysis under varied prompts, availability of human text to continue, models, and decoding strategies; statistics not described on the page.
relevant_findings: Key differentiators appear robust to generation conditions (abstract).
Genre exerts a stronger influence on stylistic features than the source; chat variants of a model cluster together; model matters more than decoding strategy, with exceptions.
limitations: Preprint without a listed venue; no numbers or unit sizes on the page.
Whether any genre is technical documentation is unknown.

decision.scope: Three design hypotheses: stratify by role before comparing sources; treat chat variants of one model as one family; hold out one generator family. No data or feature implementation is reused.
decision.reason: Directly motivates the role-first design; its own results stay hypotheses until the technical corpus is measured.
